claims.text: The starting material is an equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi elemental powder mixture.
The starting powder has no pre-existing lattice strain or nanocrystalline structure.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling produces a critical level of lattice strain.
Six hours of high-energy ball milling refines CoCrFeNiTi to a nanocrystalline grain size.
Milling-induced strain and grain refinement lower the activation-energy barrier for an FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
HEAs can form FCC or BCC solid solutions, making an FCC/BCC phase outcome plausible in principle.
Accumulated strain energy alters the Gibbs free-energy landscape so that BCC is favored over equilibrium FCC in CoCrFeNiTi.
VEC and atomic-radius mismatch govern the FCC-to-BCC phase stability in CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling effectively lowers the VEC threshold required for the FCC-to-BCC transition.
SPS at 1000°C provides sufficiently rapid diffusion to densify the milled alloy.
The specified 1000°C SPS treatment will produce greater than 98% relative density.
SPS at 1000°C avoids significant Ti-rich HCP precipitation.
The sintered alloy will retain a dominant BCC or mixed BCC+FCC solid solution.
The nanocrystalline microstructure will have higher hardness because of Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening.
Retained milling strain will additionally increase hardness through strain hardening.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi has a coarse dendritic microstructure, Ti-rich segregation, low hardness, and residual porosity.
Above 1050°C, Ti diffusion triggers HCP precipitation and rapid grain growth that degrade mechanical properties.
Low-load Vickers testing can isolate grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The boundary predicts that treatment above 1050°C should cause excessive grain growth or phase decomposition and reduce hardness, but the falsification rule says that observing lower hardness at 1100°C for exactly those reasons would falsify rather than support the predicted boundary.
